title: Lesson 8: Choosing What to Own: When a One-Off Is Better Than a Workflow
description: Choosing what to own: the discipline of deciding when a task deserves a workflow and when a one-off is the better choice, priced by build cost plus maintenance cost.

questions.question: What is the full cost of owning a workflow?
options: The build cost plus the ongoing effort to keep it working
The license fee for the software that runs the workflow
The one-time build cost alone, paid once at the very start
The training needed to teach a colleague to run the workflow
questions.explanation: A workflow is usually priced by its build, but owning it also carries a recurring maintenance cost. Inputs, tools, and the task drift, so the workflow needs periodic review and repair.

questions.question: Why can an unmaintained workflow create more risk than a one-off?
options: Because it runs longer and uses more of the tool's capacity
Because it cannot be edited once it has been saved
Because you trust it while its accuracy silently drifts down
Because one-off prompts are always more accurate than workflows
questions.explanation: A one-off is openly temporary, so you re-examine the task each time. A workflow that looks permanent invites you to stop checking, and that is when drift goes unnoticed.

questions.question: A task recurs weekly and saves about twenty minutes each run. Building the setup takes one hour, once. By the break-even question, what should you conclude?
options: The setup is never repaid, because a one-time build is a permanent loss
The setup is repaid after roughly three runs, so it creates value
The setup is repaid only if the task also changes shape each run
The setup cannot be judged without knowing the tool's monthly fee
questions.explanation: Break-even compares the build effort against the saving per run. Twenty minutes saved weekly repays a one-hour build in about three runs, and every run after that is profit.
